interview_metadata.name: John Marquette
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Angier, North Carolina, working-class all the way. My daddy worked maintenance and driving work, and Mama did bookkeeping and office work when she could, so we were never fancy but we were steady. Childhood was church suppers, tobacco fields around us, high school football on Friday nights, and learning that if something broke you tried to fix it before you complained. I was the kind of boy who liked maps, old photos, and taking apart bicycles to see how they ran. I finished high school and went on for an associate degree, mostly because I wanted practical skills and could not afford to drift around. I got into courier work young, first as a driver doing medical documents and parts runs, then more regular delivery routes around Johnston, Harnett, Wake, and Cumberland counties. I married my wife, Diane, in my late twenties, and we built a modest life in Benson. We raised two children, Emily and Mark, who are grown now. The big themes in my life have been staying dependable, trying to keep my curiosity alive, and lately trying to turn what I know about logistics into something bigger, like supervising routes or helping build a cleaner local delivery service.

follow_ups.question: What part of your childhood in Angier still shows up in your life today?
follow_ups.response: The self-reliance, for sure. I keep tools in the truck, I garden because I like knowing where food came from, and I still believe neighbors ought to know each other by name.

follow_ups.question: When did you first realize route work suited you?
follow_ups.response: Probably in my early twenties. I liked the puzzle of getting six stops done in four towns without wasting a mile, and I liked being trusted to show up on time.

follow_ups.question: What major life event changed your priorities most?
follow_ups.response: Having children changed everything. Before that I could chase overtime without thinking, but once Emily was born I started measuring success by whether I was home for supper and whether the bills were covered.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: One crossroads was after my associate degree. I had a chance to move toward a desk job in Raleigh, basic administrative work, or keep driving courier routes. The desk job looked more respectable on paper, but I had already learned I was good at time, distance, and people depending on me. Diane and I talked it over at the kitchen table, and I chose courier work because it paid quicker and gave me a path to build real expertise. Years later, that choice meant I knew back roads, customer habits, vehicle maintenance, and dispatch software in a way a manager who only saw spreadsheets might not. I sometimes wonder if I should have gone straight for a bachelor's degree, but I do not regret learning the business from the pavement up.

follow_ups.question: Who helped you think through that decision?
follow_ups.response: Diane most of all. My father told me to pick work where my word would matter, and that stuck with me too.

follow_ups.question: What did that decision cost you?
follow_ups.response: It cost me some upward mobility early on. I watched younger folks with four-year degrees move into offices faster than I did.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious. I had two offers and made lists, mileage, pay, insurance, commute, the whole thing. I am an over-planner by nature, so even when life surprises me I usually try to draw a route through it.

follow_ups.question: Do you still make decisions that way?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I use notebooks, spreadsheets, even paper maps if I am planning a trip.

follow_ups.question: Has over-planning ever worked against you?
follow_ups.response: Sure. Diane will tell you I can turn a simple Saturday drive into a military operation.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A career counselor who knew trades and logistics might have helped. Community college gave me basics, but nobody really explained how to turn delivery work into management until much later.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Clear advising on degrees, certifications, and supervisory tracks.

follow_ups.question: Do you try to give that help now?
follow_ups.response: I do with younger drivers. I tell them to learn software and customer service, not just the steering wheel.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Diane, and we have been married close to thirty years. She works part time at a dental office in town, handling front desk and insurance paperwork. We have two grown children. Emily is 28 and teaches elementary school over near Fuquay-Varina, and Mark is 24 and works in HVAC service out of Raleigh. Emily is married and has a little girl, Clara, so I am a granddaddy now. Mark is single and comes by when his schedule lets him, usually to do laundry, eat, and talk trucks. My wife and I are close, though she is more spontaneous than I am, which is probably good for me. Sunday supper is still the family anchor when we can get everybody together.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your children?
follow_ups.response: Emily maybe twice a month in person, more by phone. Mark swings through every couple of weeks, sometimes more if work is slow.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Diane do together during a normal week?
follow_ups.response: We cook together a couple nights, watch a show, go to church some Sundays, and take walks when my knees feel decent.

follow_ups.question: What is being a grandfather like for you?
follow_ups.response: It has softened me some. Clara likes my postcards and asks me to paint little houses, and that just about gets me every time.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My mother is still living in Angier in a small place near my sister Linda. My father passed about nine years ago. Linda and I are close enough to check in weekly, though we can fuss about politics.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your mother?
follow_ups.response: Usually every other weekend, and I call her Wednesdays.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your sister rely on each other for?
follow_ups.response: Mostly keeping Mama cared for and sharing family news.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a few steady friends rather than a big crowd. Ray works with me and bowls with me once a month. Walter is from my book club, and we argue about science fiction like it matters to national security. At the local museum where I volunteer, I have gotten close to Mrs. Albright, who knows more county history than anybody I have met. I also know a couple photographers around Benson who will text me when the light looks good after a storm.

follow_ups.question: How often does the book club meet?
follow_ups.response: Every Thursday evening at the library, unless weather or holidays knock it out.

follow_ups.question: What does friendship look like for you?
follow_ups.response: Showing up. Helping move a piece of furniture, checking in after a doctor visit, bringing tomatoes when the garden is heavy.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Benson, North Carolina, ZIP 27504, in a modest neighborhood with older ranch houses, some newer builds, and yards big enough for gardens. It is close enough to I-95 and I-40 that you hear traffic patterns if the wind is right, but it still feels like a small town. People wave from porches, and most everybody knows which dogs belong where. Downtown has changed some, with more antique shops and events, but it still has that working-town feel. I like being near country roads because I can get photographs of barns, fields, and tree lines without driving far.

follow_ups.question: Who are the neighbors you interact with most?
follow_ups.response: The Parkers next door and Mr. Jenkins across the street. We trade garden produce and keep an eye on packages.

follow_ups.question: What places in town do you use most?
follow_ups.response: The library, the hardware store, the barbecue place, church, and the museum.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. We lock doors and do common-sense things, but I walk early mornings without worrying much. The main safety issue is speeding on side roads.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that worried you?
follow_ups.response: A few car break-ins a couple years back, mostly unlocked vehicles.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with packages, storms, and older folks.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is community and space. The downside is you drive for many things, and growth is bringing traffic and higher costs. Still, Benson suits me better than Raleigh would.

follow_ups.question: What growth do you notice most?
follow_ups.response: More subdivisions, more trucks, and land being sold off.

follow_ups.question: What would you improve?
follow_ups.response: Better sidewalks and safer crossings near the main roads.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me and Diane in the house. We have the two bedrooms we use, one as a guest room and one partly as my art and postcard room. No one is staying temporarily. Our children visit but they do not live with us. The house is quieter than it used to be, which took some getting used to, but I admit I like having a little space for painting.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household responsibilities?
follow_ups.response: Diane handles a lot of bills and appointments, I handle yard, vehicles, most repairs, and a fair amount of cooking.

follow_ups.question: What does the guest room get used for?
follow_ups.response: Clara naps there sometimes, and Mark uses it if he stays late.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent, just me and Diane.

follow_ups.question: No short-term guests right now?
follow_ups.response: No, nobody right now.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect anyone to move in soon?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Our granddaughter Clara may stay for an overnight, and Mark sometimes crashes in the guest room.

follow_ups.question: How often does Clara stay?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two.

follow_ups.question: How often does Mark stay?
follow_ups.response: A few times a year.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: Any college students tied to the household?
follow_ups.response: No, our children are grown and on their own.

follow_ups.question: Any hospital stays in the household right now?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am usually up by 5:30, coffee by 5:45, check weather and route notes, then out the door around 6:30. Workdays vary by route, but I am usually delivering documents, parts, small freight, or specialty packages until midafternoon. Tuesday evenings I usually tend the garden or do vehicle checks. Thursday is book club. Saturday morning I walk the trail near the Benson country club area or go photograph rural scenes if the light is good. Sundays are slower, church some weeks, family supper when schedules line up, and Panthers football in season.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually get home from work?
follow_ups.response: Between 3:30 and 5:00 depending on route changes.

follow_ups.question: When do you make art?
follow_ups.response: Usually after supper, maybe 8:00 to 9:30, two or three nights a week.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a courier and messenger for a regional delivery company. We handle time-sensitive local and regional deliveries: legal packets, medical office materials, machine parts, and small business shipments. I work mostly weekdays, roughly 7:00 to 4:00, though pickups can push later. I use dispatch software, GPS, old-fashioned route knowledge, and a lot of phone communication. Lately I have also been helping with route optimization ideas and an eco-friendly delivery pilot using more efficient routing and possibly electric vehicles.

follow_ups.question: What is the most important skill in your job?
follow_ups.response: Judgment. GPS helps, but knowing when to trust it and when to take the old road matters.

follow_ups.question: Who do you report to?
follow_ups.response: A dispatch manager named Carla and an operations supervisor named Ben.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my mother with errands every other weekend, usually groceries, pharmacy, or small repairs. I volunteer at the local art and history museum two Saturdays a month, mostly cataloging postcards, labels, and small exhibits. I keep our vehicles maintained because I do not like surprises on the road. I also bowl in a senior league once a month and do crossword puzzles most nights before bed.

follow_ups.question: What do you do at the museum specifically?
follow_ups.response: I help sort donated photographs and postcards, write simple descriptions, and sometimes hang local art.

follow_ups.question: How much time does caregiving for your mother take?
follow_ups.response: Usually half a Saturday, plus a couple phone calls during the week.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is I have started taking online business classes in the evenings, one class at a time, because I want to finish a bachelor's degree eventually. That has squeezed my painting time some. At work, we have been testing new dispatch software, so I spend more time logging delivery details than I used to. I have also become more disciplined about walking because sitting and driving all day catches up with you at 57.

follow_ups.question: When do you do coursework?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Monday and Wednesday nights from about 7:30 to 9:00.

follow_ups.question: What class are you taking now?
follow_ups.response: A basic business management course.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown, so I am not managing school routines now. When they were younger, mornings were lunches, backpacks, and getting them to school before I started routes. Emily did art club and later worked at a library after school. Mark played baseball for a while and then got interested in engines. These days Emily is the one managing school routines as a teacher and mother.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with your granddaughter's routine?
follow_ups.response: Only occasionally, like pickup if Emily is in a bind.

follow_ups.question: What did you enjoy about that stage?
follow_ups.response: Evenings at ball fields and school programs. Tiring, but you knew where your effort was going.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have mostly been routine traffic stops or seeing officers through delivery work. I have been pulled over for a taillight and once for rolling a stop sign years ago, nothing dramatic. As a courier, I have delivered to courthouses and government offices, so I know some deputies by face. I respect the job, but I also know people can have very different experiences depending on who they are and where they are stopped.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt mistreated by police?
follow_ups.response: No, not personally.

follow_ups.question: Do you know officers socially?
follow_ups.response: A couple casually through church and town events, not close friends.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A wreck on I-95 stands out. I was behind a multi-car accident, and the trooper handled it calmly while traffic was a mess. I remember thinking training matters when everybody is scared.

follow_ups.question: Were you involved in the wreck?
follow_ups.response: No, just delayed and close enough to see the response.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect how you drive?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made me more careful about following distance.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I had a cousin arrested for a DUI years ago, and it shook the family up. He got through it, but it was expensive and embarrassing.

follow_ups.question: Did that change family behavior around drinking?
follow_ups.response: For a while, yes. Folks got more serious about designated drivers.

follow_ups.question: Any close family incarceration?
follow_ups.response: No close family prison time.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote pretty regularly, especially presidential, governor, county, and town elections. I missed a primary once or twice when work ran long, but I do not like skipping elections. Local offices matter to me because roads, zoning, schools, and emergency services show up in daily life. I usually read sample ballots ahead of time and talk with Diane, though we do not always vote the same way.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Early voting if I can, because routes can change.

follow_ups.question: What local issues get your attention?
follow_ups.response: Road maintenance, school funding, growth planning, and small business support.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself a moderate Republican or maybe a conservative-leaning independent, depending on the year. I grew up around people who valued work, church, personal responsibility, and not wasting public money, and I still believe in those things. But I am not interested in shouting politics or pretending every problem can be solved by saying government is bad. Roads, schools, disaster response, veterans' care, and health systems need competent public institutions. I am pro small business, skeptical of big promises, and I think taxes should be spent carefully. At the same time, I support practical environmental steps like electric delivery vehicles if they save money and reduce pollution. Socially, I am more live-and-let-live than some folks I grew up with. I do not fit neatly in one cable news box.

follow_ups.question: What issue makes you feel most conservative?
follow_ups.response: Budget discipline and the idea that work should be rewarded.

follow_ups.question: What issue makes you break from conservatives around you?
follow_ups.response: Climate and clean transportation. I think ignoring efficiency and pollution is shortsighted.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss politics often?
follow_ups.response: Only with people who can stay civil. I do not enjoy performative arguing.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten less patient with party loyalty for its own sake. The pandemic, supply chain issues, and local growth made me value competence more than slogans. I also pay more attention to infrastructure and workforce training now, because I see how fragile delivery systems can be. I still lean right on spending, but I am more open to public-private solutions and environmental investments that prove themselves.

follow_ups.question: What changed your mind on environmental investment?
follow_ups.response: Fuel prices and route data. Efficiency is not sentimental; it is math.

follow_ups.question: Has your family noticed these changes?
follow_ups.response: Diane says I have become more practical and less tribal.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say it affected me somewhat. I am a white man from central North Carolina, so I know I have not carried the same worries other people carry. At first I was skeptical of some of the protest language, but the more I listened, especially to coworkers and younger folks, the more I understood that people were talking about patterns, not just one incident. It made me think more carefully about traffic stops, sentencing, and how institutions treat people differently.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: A Black coworker named Darnell talked about being stopped in ways I have never experienced.

follow_ups.question: Did your views change quickly or slowly?
follow_ups.response: Slowly. I had to get past defensiveness.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issues deserve attention: unequal treatment, excessive force, and trust between communities and police. I do not agree with every slogan or tactic, but that does not mean the problem is imaginary. My practical side wants better training, body cameras used properly, accountability, and also support for officers doing mental health calls they are not equipped for. I think rural and small-town people need to talk about this too, not just big cities.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any behavior because of these conversations?
follow_ups.response: I listen more before I give an opinion, especially around coworkers.

follow_ups.question: What makes the conversation hard?
follow_ups.response: People hear criticism of systems as criticism of every individual officer or every white person.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is woven into history more than some people want to admit. Around here, you can see it in neighborhoods, schools, land ownership, and who had chances to build wealth. I am not someone who thinks every conversation needs to become a lecture, but I do think honest local history matters. Volunteering at the museum has made that clearer because old photographs and records show what was included and what got left out.

follow_ups.question: Has museum work affected your view of race?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Archives show whose stories were preserved and whose were ignored.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with older relatives?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. Some listen, some shut it down.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family, coworkers, and book club friends, but I have not joined protests. I have tried to include more complete local history in museum displays when I have a say.

follow_ups.question: What kinds of conversations happen at book club?
follow_ups.response: Usually careful but honest, especially when a novel touches race or policing.

follow_ups.question: Why no protests?
follow_ups.response: Partly schedule, partly temperament. I am more comfortable doing local work quietly.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Diane is pretty compassionate and thinks people should be heard. My son Mark is more skeptical and gets tired of what he calls politics in everything. Emily, being a teacher, thinks schools need to tell history more honestly and treat families fairly. My sister Linda is more conservative than me and sees the topic as divisive. So inside my own family there is a range.

follow_ups.question: Do disagreements get heated?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially with Linda, but we usually back off before it damages anything.

follow_ups.question: Who do you find easiest to talk with?
follow_ups.response: Emily. She is thoughtful and deals with children and families every day.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say I am in decent health for 57, but not invincible. I have borderline high blood pressure that I watch, some knee stiffness from years of driving and climbing in and out of vans, and I could stand to lose 15 pounds. I walk weekly and try to stretch, but I still enjoy barbecue and biscuits more than a doctor would prefer. I see a primary care doctor once or twice a year and get routine bloodwork.

follow_ups.question: Are you taking regular medication?
follow_ups.response: A low-dose blood pressure medicine and occasional ibuprofen for knee pain.

follow_ups.question: What health habit are you proudest of?
follow_ups.response: Walking consistently and not smoking.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Having trails nearby and a garden makes it easier. My job makes it harder because driving means sitting, eating on the go, and odd meal times. Diane helps by cooking vegetables, and I help by growing tomatoes, basil, peppers, and squash. Stress and time are the enemies.

follow_ups.question: What do you eat on workdays?
follow_ups.response: I pack sandwiches or leftovers when I am disciplined; otherwise it is gas station coffee and something regrettable.

follow_ups.question: How often do you walk?
follow_ups.response: Usually once long walk a week and shorter walks when I can.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No major diagnosis like cancer or diabetes, thank goodness. My doctor did flag my blood pressure and cholesterol as things to control, so I have been trying to improve those. Last year I had a knee flare-up after a long route with too many stairs, and I did a few physical therapy visits. It reminded me that I cannot treat my body like a delivery van with unlimited mileage.

follow_ups.question: Did physical therapy help?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially strengthening exercises and learning how to stretch properly.

follow_ups.question: Did you miss work?
follow_ups.response: Only one day, then I adjusted routes for a bit.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My knee can slow me down, but it has not kept me from working in a serious way. I plan routes to avoid unnecessary stairs when possible and use a hand truck more than pride would like.

follow_ups.question: Does your employer accommodate that?
follow_ups.response: Informally, yes. Dispatch knows I can do the work if routes are sensible.

follow_ups.question: Does pain affect home life?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I skip yard work after a hard route.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My mother has arthritis and some memory slips, nothing officially severe yet, but enough that Linda and I watch closely. Diane had a scare with a breast biopsy a few years back that turned out benign, and that made us both grateful for screenings. I also help my mother manage medicines because bottles and refill dates can get confusing.

follow_ups.question: Who coordinates your mother's care?
follow_ups.response: Linda handles most appointments because she lives closer, and I handle errands and repairs.

follow_ups.question: Has caregiving affected your schedule?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly weekends and phone calls.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have employer insurance, but deductibles and copays still make you think twice. I have delayed dental work once because the estimate was high. Diane is good at navigating insurance because of her job, which helps a lot. Getting appointments is not terrible for primary care, but specialists can take weeks.

follow_ups.question: Have you skipped prescriptions?
follow_ups.response: No, not prescriptions.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest about the system?
follow_ups.response: Understanding what something will cost before you agree to it.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing too exotic. We use heating pads, Epsom salt soaks, herbal tea, and my mother swears by menthol rub. I have tried turmeric capsules for joint stiffness, but I still rely on regular doctors for real medical decisions. Around here, home remedies are part of culture, but I do not confuse them with emergency care.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those remedies?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Mama and older church ladies.

follow_ups.question: Do you tell your doctor about supplements?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially after Diane reminded me interactions can matter.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke and never really did beyond trying it as a teenager. I drink lightly, maybe a beer during a Panthers game or a glass of wine if Diane and I go out. During tough times I am more likely to over-plan, clean the garage, or listen to jazz than drink heavily. I have seen alcohol cause trouble in families, so I keep a short leash on it.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when stress peaks?
follow_ups.response: I take a drive without deliveries attached, or I paint with Miles Davis playing.

follow_ups.question: Any drinking in the past week?
follow_ups.response: One beer on Saturday evening.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: No marijuana or other drugs. I take prescribed blood pressure medicine, and I use over-the-counter ibuprofen when my knee acts up. The most recent was probably last Thursday after a route with a lot of steps; I took two ibuprofen with supper and iced the knee. I am cautious because I know pain pills can become a problem.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever used opioid pain medication?
follow_ups.response: Only briefly after dental surgery years ago, exactly as prescribed.

follow_ups.question: Do you use sleep aids?
follow_ups.response: No, just reading or crosswords to wind down.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We use my employer insurance and Diane's knowledge from the dental office to avoid billing surprises when we can. We budget monthly for prescriptions, copays, and dental visits. If something big came up, we would use savings first, then maybe a payment plan. It is manageable right now but not something you ignore.

follow_ups.question: Do you have an emergency medical fund?
follow_ups.response: Not separate, but part of general savings.

follow_ups.question: Do your adult children rely on you for health costs?
follow_ups.response: No, not regularly.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I got COVID shots and boosters recommended for my age, and I get a flu shot most years. I read up first, but I trust mainstream medical advice more than social media rumors.

follow_ups.response: Responsibility. Sometimes pride, sometimes worry.

transcript.response: Last fall my mother got confused about a prescription and took the wrong dose for a couple days. She was okay, but it scared me. I drove to Angier after work, and on the way I felt guilty that I had not checked sooner. That night Linda and I sat at Mama's table making a medicine chart. follow_ups.question: Did you tell Diane how you felt?

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Daddy worked maintenance and delivery for a building supply company. He drove materials, repaired equipment, loaded trucks, and kept things running. He knew engines, tools, and back roads.

follow_ups.question: Did his work influence yours?

follow_ups.question: What did he teach you directly?

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: It was a local building supply and hardware business. They sold lumber, concrete mix, roofing, tools, and delivered materials to job sites and farms.

follow_ups.question: Was it physically demanding?

follow_ups.question: Did he know customers well?

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am in a supervisory logistics role, not just driving every mile myself. I want to help build smarter routes, mentor younger couriers, and prove that cleaner delivery can work in a place like Harnett County. I hope to finish my bachelor's degree, even if slowly. Personally, I want Diane and me healthy enough to travel more: Blue Ridge weekends, Charleston again, and maybe Provence in spring if we can save for it. I want to keep painting and photographing North Carolina before more old barns and storefronts disappear. Mostly I want to be useful without running myself into the ground.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Finishing my current business class and documenting results from the route pilot.

follow_ups.question: What do you hope stays the same?
follow_ups.response: Family dinners, the garden, and living in a place where people know us.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, dependability, curiosity, and doing work that has some dignity. I value the land and local history because they remind me I am not floating loose in the world. I value honesty, but not cruelty dressed up as honesty. If people remember me as someone who showed up, kept his word, helped younger folks learn, and left behind a few good paintings or photographs, that would be enough.

follow_ups.question: Which value do you practice daily?
follow_ups.response: Dependability. Being where I said I would be, when I said I would be there.

follow_ups.question: What do you want your grandchildren to learn from you?
follow_ups.response: Pay attention, be kind, and take care of what has been trusted to you.
